text:
Mississippi offered her a way out of prison for $200. She refused to pay—and spent two months on death row for challenging racial segregation.

In 1961, Joan Trumpauer Mulholland was 19 when she joined the Freedom Riders, who were testing the enforcement of desegregation on interstate buses and in terminals. 

Raised white in segregated Virginia, she could have stayed quiet and kept the advantages her skin color gave her. Instead she joined sit-ins and protests against Jim Crow.

On June 8, 1961, she was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, and sent to Parchman Penitentiary. There she and other female Freedom Riders were held in maximum-security cells on death row. 

The state set a $200 fine. She could have paid it and left. She refused.

Joan and the others faced overcrowded cells, extreme summer heat, harsh conditions, and pressure meant to break them. 

They sang freedom songs to hold their spirits together, even when guards tried to stop them. After about two months she finished her sentence without paying the fine.

Prison did not end her work. That fall she enrolled at Tougaloo College, a historically Black college in Mississippi, and kept organizing for civil rights. 

She later helped with the 1963 March on Washington. The Ku Klux Klan targeted her, yet she continued standing with those fighting for equality.

Her 1961 booking photograph is now in the Library of Congress—a record of a young woman who challenged an unjust system when silence would have been easier. 

She entered prison at 19 because she believed equality was worth the cost. She left without giving up that belief. 🌹

Last week, Marco Rubio (@SecRubio), the US Secretary of State, posted an offer to people inside Cuba. "Now is the time," he wrote, to create change "through a discrete partnership with the CIA."

I met Rubio once. In 2017, when I was 17, he showed up at my high school by himself. Someone said he was there to see a friend. His parents left Cuba in 1956, and opposing the government Castro set up is what he's built his career on.

Moments before the post, President Trump was at a rally in Florida, talking about warships on their way back from Iran that would stop "about 50 yards off the coast" of Cuba. Then, he said, Rubio would go in "to finish up the deal."

A rhetorically similar mix of carrot and stick is featured in a famous message from Chinese history. In December 1948, during China's civil war, Mao Zedong wrote a radio broadcast addressed to the encircled Nationalist general Du Yuming.

The message addressed Du and his commanders by name and told them, "You have come to the end of the road." It listed the Nationalist generals who had already switched sides to Mao, along with over 20,000 soldiers, and offered Du's troops one thing: to be allowed to live.

It closed with the words, "If you still want to fight, fight some more. You will be finished either way."

Du would not surrender, and he was captured a few weeks later. But Mao could be so blunt because Du's men were packed into a pocket a few miles across, and every soldier could see the army surrounding them.

Rubio does not have an army surrounding Cuba. What he does have, for now, is the oil. Since the United States cut off Cuba's supply of Venezuelan oil this year, Cuba has been short about 2,000 megawatts of power on most evenings, and some blackouts have lasted 20 hours.

In March, after 90 consecutive hours of power outages, citizens of the town of Morón stormed the local headquarters of the Communist Party. Prosecutors now want to sentence 18 people involved, six of them minors, to up to 13 years in prison.

text:
Around 524 BC, a Persian army of fifty thousand men marched west into the Egyptian desert and was never seen again. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, the soldiers were sitting down to a midday meal somewhere in the endless sand between the oases of the Western Desert when a violent wind rose out of the south. It drove walls of sand over them, burying the entire army where it sat. No survivors returned. No messengers came back. For two and a half thousand years, the Lost Army of Cambyses has been one of the great mysteries of the ancient world, chased by explorers, adventurers, and archaeologists, and the subject of a modern debate over whether the sandstorm ever happened at all.

The man who sent that army was Cambyses II, son of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian Empire. Cyrus had conquered Media, Lydia, and Babylon, building the largest empire the world had yet seen, and died fighting in Central Asia around 530 BC. Cambyses inherited his father's ambitions and turned toward the one great power of the Near East that Persia had not yet swallowed: Egypt. In 525 BC he invaded, crushed the Egyptian army at the Battle of Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, captured Memphis, and took the young pharaoh Psamtik III prisoner. Egypt became a Persian province, and Cambyses was crowned as its pharaoh.

Cambyses was not content to stop there. Herodotus says he planned three further campaigns. The first was against Carthage, the great Phoenician colony in North Africa, but it collapsed before it began because the Phoenician sailors who made up the backbone of the Persian navy refused to make war on their own colonists. The second was a massive expedition south up the Nile against the kingdom the Greeks called Ethiopia, meaning Kush in what is now Sudan, which Cambyses led himself. The third was the expedition west into the desert against the Ammonians, the people of the oasis now called Siwa, home of the famous oracle of the god Amun.

The Ethiopian campaign is worth pausing on, because it shows how Herodotus wanted his readers to see Cambyses. Before marching, Cambyses sent spies to the Ethiopian king disguised as envoys bearing gifts. The king saw through them at once. He handed them an enormous bow and told them to carry a message back to their master: when the Persians could draw a bow that size as easily as the Ethiopians did, they could come and attack, and until then they should thank the gods that the Ethiopians had no desire to conquer other people's lands. Cambyses, Herodotus says, flew into a rage and marched south immediately, without preparing proper supplies. Before the army had covered a fifth of the distance, the food ran out. The soldiers ate their pack animals, then grass, and then, in the desert, they began drawing lots to choose one man in every ten to be eaten by his comrades. Only then did Cambyses turn back.

The army sent against the Ammonians suffered a stranger fate. Herodotus says Cambyses detached fifty thousand men from his force at Thebes, in Upper Egypt, with orders to enslave the Ammonians and burn the oracle of Amun. The army set out with guides and reached a place Herodotus calls the city of Oasis, seven days' march across the sand from Thebes. Historians generally identify this with the Kharga Oasis in the Western Desert, which the Greeks poetically called the Islands of the Blessed. The army is known to have reached that point. Beyond it, Herodotus admits, no one except the Ammonians and those who heard their account knew what happened. The soldiers never reached Siwa, and they never came back to Egypt.

The story the Ammonians told was the sandstorm. As the army marched from the oasis toward Siwa, somewhere roughly midway between the two, the men halted for their morning meal. Then a powerful south wind came roaring across the desert, carrying heaps of sand, and buried the army completely. And that, Herodotus says, was how the expedition against the Ammonians ended.

The story fit neatly into the larger portrait Herodotus painted of Cambyses as a madman who offended the gods. He claims Cambyses mocked Egyptian religion, desecrated tombs, and in a fit of madness stabbed the sacred Apis bull of Memphis in the thigh, causing it to die. An army sent to destroy the oracle of a god and swallowed by the desert before it got there is exactly the kind of divine punishment that ran through Greek storytelling. It is worth knowing, though, that Herodotus's picture of Cambyses was heavily colored by hostile Egyptian priests and by Persian propaganda from the regime that followed him. Archaeology has contradicted some of it directly. At the Serapeum in Saqqara, the underground burial complex for the Apis bulls, excavators found an inscription recording that an Apis bull was buried with full honors during Cambyses's reign, and the king himself is shown kneeling in respect before it. That does not prove every charge false, but it is a strong warning against taking Herodotus's account of Cambyses at face value.

Meanwhile, the idea of fifty thousand soldiers lying entombed beneath the dunes, with their weapons, armor, and treasure perfectly preserved, proved irresistible to treasure hunters and explorers. Expeditions have gone looking since at least the nineteenth century. In the 1930s, the Hungarian desert explorer László Almásy, the real figure behind the main character of the novel and film The English Patient, was among those drawn to the mystery as he crisscrossed the Western Desert. Others have followed with camels, trucks, aircraft, and satellite imagery. Every so often, someone announces a breakthrough.

The most famous announcement came in 2009, when two Italian twin brothers, Angelo and Alfredo Castiglioni, documentary filmmakers and archaeological explorers, said they had found evidence of the army in the Western Desert. They reported bronze weapons, a silver bracelet, an earring, and human bones, along with a natural rock shelter where they believed soldiers may have sought refuge from the storm. The news spread around the world. But many archaeologists were skeptical. The finds were scattered and undated, scattered bones and artifacts turn up throughout the desert from many periods, and Egyptian antiquities officials stated that the work had not been carried out under an official permit. The claim has never been confirmed, and most specialists do not regard it as proof of the lost army.

The deeper problem is the story itself. Experienced desert travelers and geologists have pointed out that while sandstorms in the Western Desert are ferocious, they do not usually bury large numbers of people where they stand. A storm can blind travelers, scatter caravans, destroy supplies, and leave people lost to die of thirst, but entombing an entire army of tens of thousands in a single blow is very hard to imagine. The figure of fifty thousand men also strains belief. Moving and watering an army that size across hundreds of kilometers of waterless desert would have been an enormous logistical challenge, and ancient numbers for armies are notoriously inflated.

In 2014, the Dutch Egyptologist Olaf Kaper of Leiden University proposed a different explanation, one that turns the story from a natural disaster into a military defeat. Studying temple inscriptions at the Dakhla Oasis, west of Kharga, Kaper reconstructed the reign of a little known Egyptian rebel leader named Petubastis, who claimed the title of pharaoh around this time and appears to have been based in the oases of the Western Desert. Kaper argues that Cambyses's army was not marching on Siwa at all, or not only, but was sent to crush this rebel, and that Petubastis's forces ambushed and destroyed it somewhere in the desert. A few years later, the rebellion was put down by the Persian king Darius I, who seized the throne after Cambyses died in 522 BC. In Kaper's view, the story of a supernatural sandstorm may have been a convenient way to explain away a humiliating Persian defeat at the hands of an Egyptian rebel, and Darius's regime had no interest in advertising that one of its armies had been wiped out by a local uprising. Kaper's theory is not universally accepted, and the evidence is thin, but it offers a plausible explanation for why the army disappeared, why the Ammonians had a story about it, and why the official record was so silent.

Whatever happened, the fate of the army seems to have done nothing to hurt the oracle it was sent to destroy. If anything, its reputation grew. Two centuries later, in 332 BC, Alexander the Great made a famous and dangerous march across the desert to Siwa to consult the oracle of Amun himself. According to the ancient historians of his campaign, his column was nearly lost when water ran out and sandstorms obscured the route, until rain fell unexpectedly and birds or, in some versions, serpents guided the Macedonians to the oasis. There, the priests greeted Alexander as the son of Amun, a moment that profoundly shaped how he saw himself for the rest of his life. Alexander's writers clearly had the fate of Cambyses's army in mind, and the contrast was the point: the Persian king who came to destroy the god's shrine was swallowed by the desert, while the Macedonian who came to honor it was led safely through.

The Lost Army of Cambyses remains lost. It may lie under the sand somewhere between Kharga and Siwa, as the Ammonians claimed. It may have been cut down by rebels and its story rewritten by a new king who preferred a tale of divine wrath to an admission of defeat. Or it may have been far smaller than Herodotus believed, simply dying of thirst and disorientation in one of the harshest landscapes on earth. What survives is one of the most enduring legends of the ancient world: an imperial army marching into the desert to destroy a god's oracle, and the desert closing over it as if it had never been.

Switzerland: The Profitable Business of Neutrality

Switzerland is famous for flawless chocolate, precise watches, and supposedly crystal-clear neutrality. Yet during World War II, that neutrality had a distinct taste of gun oil, steel, and gold bullion.

The charming story of a small Alpine republic surviving among ruthless dictatorships through courage and mountains alone is comforting. Reality was considerably more complicated — and profitable.

After France collapsed in 1940, Switzerland found itself surrounded by Axis-controlled territory. Rather than confront Nazi Germany, its government pursued a pragmatic strategy: maintain economic relations while preparing for a possible invasion.

Swiss factories supplied Germany with weapons, precision instruments, machinery, and industrial components. The logic was simple: a functioning Swiss economy could be more valuable to Berlin than an occupied country.

Switzerland also maintained vital railway connections through the Alps between Germany and Italy. Neutrality, apparently, did not prevent business from running on schedule.

Consider Oerlikon-Bührle, a major Swiss arms manufacturer whose wartime dealings became the subject of historical controversy. Questions surrounding corporate records and profits illustrate how uncomfortable the financial history of neutrality could become.

Meanwhile, General Henri Guisan prepared the Swiss Army to resist an invasion from fortified Alpine positions known as the National Redoubt.

Ordinary soldiers were expected to defend their country at enormous personal risk. Industrialists and bankers, meanwhile, continued conducting business with the very dictatorship those soldiers might eventually have to fight.

An extraordinary division of labor: patriotism in the mountains, profits in the boardrooms.

The financial relationship was even more troubling.

Nazi Germany desperately needed convertible currency. Switzerland offered something invaluable: a stable franc, sophisticated banking institutions, and access to international financial transactions.

The Swiss National Bank purchased substantial quantities of gold from Germany's Reichsbank, including gold that Nazi authorities had stolen from occupied countries.

Gold could be melted down. Its origins could be obscured. And money, unlike human conscience, rarely asks difficult questions.

The Allies increasingly recognized the problem. By 1944, Washington's Operation Safehaven was investigating Nazi assets and financial networks in neutral countries, including Switzerland.

The concern was not merely wartime commerce. Allied governments feared that stolen wealth could survive Germany's defeat and help Nazi networks preserve their economic influence.

After 1945, Switzerland emphasized its military preparedness, humanitarian activities, and determination to preserve independence.

Those achievements were real. So were its economic dealings with the Third Reich.

For decades, the heroic narrative received far more attention than the uncomfortable financial evidence. Only later did major investigations, including the Bergier Commission, systematically examine Switzerland's wartime economic relationships and refugee policies.

The resulting historical picture was neither simple heroism nor complete collaboration. Switzerland faced genuine threats of invasion and severe economic pressure. But some Swiss businesses and financial institutions also benefited from transactions that helped sustain Nazi Germany.

And that distinction matters.

A country may make painful compromises to survive. But survival does not automatically erase responsibility for those compromises.

Switzerland's greatest historical problem is not simply that it traded with Nazi Germany while surrounded by Axis powers.

It is how long the comforting legend of spotless neutrality overshadowed the far less comfortable truth.

Because neutrality may keep a country out of a war.

It does not necessarily keep its money out of one.

MANUSCRIPT:
Series:  “1 Cor: Holiness from Messes” #39 
Text:  1 Corinthians 10:31–11:1
By:  Shaun Marksbury  
Date:  Oct. 25, 2026
Venue:  Living Water Baptist Church 
Occasion:  AM Service

Introduction
It is Reformation Day. We remember a historic act today — on October 31, 1517, Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg.  Remember that the center of the controversy of that day was the sale of indulgences (certificates that claimed to reduce the punishment of sin in exchange for money).  The Roman Catholic system taught people that they could contribute something that would help secure their standing before God.

The Reformers rightly rejected that human effort and merit could in any way earn salvation.  Instead, they insisted that if we contribute anything, then we can claim at least some of the glory.  Based on Scripture, salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone (Eph. 2:1–10). In other words, the glory belongs to God alone, a doctrine known as Soli Deo Gloria.

That is the same principle leading our text this morning.  After chapters of discussion about Christian liberty and food offered to idols, Paul concludes here with a “therefore” or “then,” and he says we should “do all to the glory of God.”  He knew the Corinthians were tempted to use their freedom for their own rights and preferences, so he redirects away from advancing themselves toward lifting high God.

Soli Deo Gloria doesn’t just help us define our salvation — it governs the Christian life. Even though there are three commands in this text, the pinnacle command tells us to do everything for God’s glory, and we’ll see three aspects of that this morning. We’ll note the principle, the practice, and the pattern of doing all to the glory of God. Let’s begin with the principle.

First, Note the Principle of Doing All to the Glory of God (10:31)
Whether, then, you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

Again, we must notice the second word here. We know that when there is a “therefore,” we must ask what that’s there for! Sometimes, though, the same underlying Greek term is translated “then.” This signals that Paul is taking his teaching (in this case, the argument of chapters 8–10) and applying it to a principle.

Before, he gave a different principle, that we should be seeking the good of others (v. 24). This is even more fundamental than that. If seeking the good of others is the second great commandment, then this is the first — to “love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22:37). This is about exalting God above all else.

Let’s consider that. Paul mentions eating and drinking, very ordinary and mundane parts of our lives. Some might think that this is about glorifying God even in the small parts of our lives, which is important. However, remember that Paul has been talking about their idolatrous use of food.[1] In the next chapter, he’ll discuss those showing up drunk at the communal gatherings (11:21)! Eating and drinking are key problems in church of Corinth.

How does Paul advise them? He doesn’t tell them to stop eating and drinking. Rather, so far, he has told them to consider whether their behavior was spiritually beneficial to themselves, whether it considered the good of other people, and now, whether it glorifies God. If we can filter our choices through these kinds of categories, then we know that we’re living in a way pleasing to God.

Yet, he isn’t binding this principle to just those two activities. He goes on to say the words “whatever you do,” universalizing the principle beyond food to other issues in this book and beyond.  As one commentator notes,

Sexual immorality (chs. 5–6) and idolatry (chs. 8–10) are the antithesis to the glorification of God.  They are to be countered by the manifestation of Christian sexual purity (ch. 7) and God-honoring worship (chs. 11–14) which reflect true wisdom (cf. chs. 1–4) as we await the return of the resurrected Son of God (ch. 15). Any behavior that detracts from God’s glory is to be rejected in favor of ones that promote it.[2]

Christian liberty is never license for self-preference — it’s about the selfless glorification of God.[3]

Okay, you might say. I understand what Paul is saying in general. But, what does it mean to glorify God?

God’s “glory” is His greatness, His worth. To glorify Him, then, is to display His excellence and honor in some way. As God says in Ezekiel 36:23, “ ‘I will prove the holiness of My great name which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst.  Then the nations will know that I am Yahweh,’ declares Lord Yahweh, ‘when I prove Myself holy among you in their sight.’ ”  To do something to the glory of God is to act in a way that makes much of Him rather than of ourselves, letting people see Him through us.

Again, this is in everything, starting with salvation. The Reformers rightly insisted that even justification is soli Deo gloria, that God said He glorifies Himself in wiping away our sins; we even glorify Him by not adding our own works to the process of salvation.  Paul makes the same point about the whole of Christian living.  We are not to make the Christian life about ourselves.

Think about this with preaching. I could stand up here, read a verse, and then spend half an hour talking about me and my family. Some people think evangelism is about getting people to like you. These things become an excuse for a selfish Christianity that doesn’t glorify God.

The Corinthians had a slogan — “all things are lawful.”  Well, Paul replaces it here with a new one: “Do all things to the glory of God.”[4]  When you seek to obey God’s word or serve other people before yourself, you are glorifying God. On the other hand, any practice that leads others to denigrate the faith or that prioritizes our rights over God’s commands dishonors Him.  Any sin causes us to fall short of this command.[5]

So, let us make this our own slogan. If you want to know more about living out this principle, then look with me at the next verse of this chapter as we come to the next point:

Second, Note the Practice of Doing All to the Glory of God (10:32)
Give no offense either to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God;

Here, we have another command — “give” — stated in the negative (“don’t give”). These verses show how the principle of 10:31 is lived in the concrete situation Paul has been addressing. They are not a separate topic; they are the application of Soli Deo Gloria in the sphere of liberty and witness.

The command is telling us to avoid giving offense to others. Now, we can’t necessarily control if someone finds what we say offensive or feels offended just by our presence or message. But that’s not what the Lord would have us consider here; we’re to avoid being offensive to others. The term means that we should avoid causing others to stumble morally or spiritually.

Think about it with unbelievers — we would become a barrier to the gospel. As one commentary notes here, “People who wish to do everything for the glory of God cannot succeed if they act in disregard for others.  Paul was always relinquishing his rights for the spiritual benefit of others — that they may be saved.”[6] Again, we aren’t responsible because someone feels bad for the preaching of the message, but we can avoid speaking in a way that purposefully offends.

This is something people who are chronically online could learn. There are people who open anonymous accounts not because of persecution but because they want to post some of the most vile content possible without consequence. This includes professing Christians, because some of them include statements like “Christ is King” in their profiles. They have become stumbling blocks at the entrance to the Kingdom of God.

Consider how Paul breaks it down here. He says to avoid offending both Jews and Greeks. Incidentally, I am shocked by how many of these professed Christians online are attacking unbelieving Jews when God’s Word here forbids it. Paul is even talking about behavior here — don’t engage in activity in front of Jews that you know will be offensive to them, like the appearance of idolatry.[7] Some point out that they are believing falsely and are unsaved, and that’s the point: we should strive to avoid being the reason they don’t come to Christ.

He doesn’t just focus on Jews, though. The “Greeks,” a term synonymous with “Gentiles,” might likewise be offended by the apparent hypocrisy of the Christians who appear to engage in idolatry with their eating habits.[8] Both the Jewish and Gentile converts were to have concern for unbelievers from either ethnicity; Christians who don’t fail to glorify God in their lives.

Paul doesn’t end with the unbeliever — he now turns to the rest of humanity by mentioning “the church of God.” The Jews who converted shouldn’t be “unnecessarily grieved nor prejudiced” against the Gentile converts or their consciences.[9] The Gentile converts should not engage in activities that a weaker Jewish brother might interpret as veneration of idols.[10] The point is the same for unbelievers and for believers: our use of liberty must not hinder others, either in their coming to or ongoing belief in the gospel.

There is all manner of idolatry. The Roman Catholics will claim that they don’t have it while venerating statues, and the Greek Orthodox can fall into it with paintings, all of which rob God of glory. People can also make idols out of their own liberties and freedoms, choosing their desires over the good of others. We Protestants can fail in this all the time.

We need to change our practice if we want to glorify God in all we do. Thankfully, we have a pattern to follow. Let’s look at the next two verses, even though that takes us into the next chapter:

Third, Note the Pattern of Doing All to the Glory of God (10:33–11:1)
just as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit but the profit of the many, so that they may be saved.  Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.

11:1 belongs with chapter 10, and maybe that makes sense as we read it together like this. Remember that the verse numbers and chapters were added later; Paul didn’t divide his writing into chapters like this! The numbers are here so we can navigate the text, and unfortunately, they sometimes fail us. Let’s consider what these verses are teaching us together.

Paul is saying that he models what it means to glorify God. He begins by saying “just as,” meaning that he intends to be copied in his behavior. He’s demonstrating a pattern.

He says he is “not seeking my own profit but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.”  Now, don’t be confused; this is not mere people-pleasing. Elsewhere, Paul warns that seeking to please other people is at odds with pleasing God (Gal 1:10). The trouble is valuing the opinions and feelings of other people over our own convictions and what God has revealed.

Here, Paul is highlighting a different problem. He warns against seeking to please ourselves above pleasing other people, valuing our own desires above others. Being a self-pleaser is just as antithetical to God’s glory as being a people-pleaser, and it can be just as deceptive. We may wrap it in terms of self-love and self-care, but it really comes down to being selfish at times.

Paul modeled setting aside his own advantages at times to seek the good of others. Paul repeatedly set aside personal advantage and safety for the sake of the gospel, including his willingness to go to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 25). In Romans 15:2, he says, “Each of us is to please his neighbor for his good, to his building up.” This is glorifying God in his life, and we should consider the model.

In 11:1, he then supplies the standard.  He gives us the final command we have today as he calls them to imitate him. How?

Christ is the ultimate example, the one Paul (and we) should imitate. Remember that in Philippians 2:4, Paul says that no one should be looking for his own interests alone, but also for the interests of others; he then tells of how Christ did this very thing (vv. 5–7). Jesus Christ was willing to set aside His own glory and advantages for the salvation of others — ultimately, through going to the cross for our sins (Isa. 53; 1 Cor. 8:11; 10:16; 15:3).

Paul sought to give up his rights for others, too, saying, “that they may be saved.” His purpose was evangelism (cf. Rom. 11:14; 1 Thess. 2:16). To be clear, the “they” here would refer both to the Jews and Gentiles of the previous verse, and if we want to follow Paul, we should seek to glorify God by being inoffensive and sharing the faith with unbelievers.

I want you to notice something else: this is a passive statement. Paul doesn’t say he does the saving, for that would also detract from God’s glory. This is a divine passive — God does the saving though our works and behavior.

Paul isn’t saying to imitate him in particular, then. He’s human with sins and imperfections. Rather, he wants the reader to imitate his imitation of Christ. Our Lord is the ultimate standard.

This is soli deo gloria. The Son seeks the Father’s glory by seeking the salvation of others at the cost of Himself.  When the Corinthians (and we) regulate our liberty by love, we are following that pattern.  The result is a life free from the tyranny of our own rights and preferences, oriented entirely toward the honor of God and the good of others.

Conclusion
Christian freedom is freedom from ourselves to glorify God by becoming like Christ.  On this Reformation Sunday, the glory of God isn’t just about your salvation — which I hope you trust in the hands of the Lord Jesus alone. It is also the practical demand of this text.

Do you live soli deo gloria? Whether the issue is food, drink, social customs, or any other use of liberty, the question is not “What am I free to do?” but “What will honor God and advance the gospel?”

May we live lives to the glory of God alone.
_______________________________

[1] Roy E. Ciampa and Brian S. Rosner, The First Letter to the Corinthians, The Pillar New Testament Commentary (Grand Rapids, MI; Cambridge, U.K.: William B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 2010), 495–496.

[2] Ibid., 496.

[3] John F. MacArthur Jr., 1 Corinthians, MacArthur New Testament Commentary (Chicago: Moody Press, 1984), 248.

[4] Andrew David Naselli, “1 Corinthians,” in Romans–Galatians, eds. Iain M. Duguid, James M. Hamilton Jr., and Jay Sklar, (Wheaton, IL: Crossway, 2020), X, 309.

The other day I walked into a job interview with 25 years of experience, a polished resume, and enough coffee to negotiate world peace. I was ready to discuss leadership and business results. Instead, I entered the championship round of Who Wants to Hire Absolutely Nobody? 

The manager asked, “If you were a fruit, what fruit would you be?” I said, “A pineapple. Tough exterior, excellent under pressure, and nobody wants to deal with me without a sharp knife.” She wrote: “Threat to produce.” The stapler nearly quit.

Then she asked, “How many golf balls fit inside a Boeing 747?” I said, “Depends. Are we still allowing passengers, or has Spirit Airlines introduced a new seating arrangement?” No laugh. “Where do you see yourself in five years?” Somewhere my career isn’t determined by airborne golf balls. “What’s your biggest weakness?” Believing job interviews might occasionally involve the job. “If you were a superhero, what would your power be?” Making recruiters respond after saying, “We’ll get back to you.” I’d be famous by Thursday.

Then came, “Sell me this pen.” I said, “It’s a pen. It writes. It’s reliable. Unlike your applicant tracking system, it actually works when someone touches it.” No smile. Next question. “If you were an animal, what would you be?” A raccoon. Adaptable, resourceful, and built for corporate dumpster fires. “How would you move Mount Everest?” I’d assign it unrealistic quarterly targets, schedule three accountability meetings, and put it on a performance improvement plan. That mountain would be in Florida by Friday.

She leaned forward. “If you were stranded on an island, what three things would you bring?” A boat, GPS, and whoever approved this interview format. We need to talk before rescue arrives. “What kitchen utensil represents your personality?” A spatula. I’ve been flipping bad situations into positive results for decades. “How do you handle stress?” I survived dial-up internet, Windows 95, fax machines, and printers that jam during executive visits. Stress should be asking me for coaching.

Finally came the question that nearly sent me under the conference table. “Why should we hire you?” You advertised a job requiring experience, leadership, and results. I brought all three. Nobody mentioned a master’s degree in fruit identification or advanced geometry for commercial aircraft. She said, “We want someone who thinks outside the box.” I said, “At this point, I’d love to meet someone who remembers what was supposed to be inside the box.”

One of America’s most notorious mobsters wasn’t brought down by a rival gangster or a hail of bullets. Instead, it was tax evasion that ultimately landed Al Capone behind bars.

In October 1931, the Chicago crime boss stood trial on federal tax evasion charges. Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors pulled back the curtain on Capone’s extravagant lifestyle, revealing his lavish spending on luxury clothing, expensive automobiles, and his Florida estate.

Al Capone's lavish spending helped expose his wealth during his 1931 tax evasion trial. Among the expenses presented in court? A $3,141 Miami telephone bill, which is equivalent to nearly $71,000 today.

But it was the smaller luxuries that offered a glimpse into Capone’s expensive tastes. Jurors learned that he purchased $12 pairs of silk underwear, favored monogrammed shirts costing as much as $27 each (nearly , and owned sterling silver dinner sets. His furniture preferences were just as distinctive, with canary yellow and green among his favorite colors.

As the trial drew to a close on Oct. 17, U.S. Attorney George E.Q. Johnson urged jurors to consider where Capone’s wealth originated. In his closing remarks, Johnson delivered a statement that captured the significance of the case: “Future generations will not remember this case because of the name Alphonse Capone, but because it will establish whether or not a man can go so far beyond that law as to be able to escape the law.”
That same day, a federal jury convicted Capone of tax evasion and related tax offenses.

On Oct. 24, 1931, Judge James H. Wilkerson handed down a staggering sentence: 10 years in federal prison, an additional year and a half of jail time, and $50,000 in fines and court costs.

“I guess it’s all over,” Capone told his attorneys. “You done all you could.”

The conviction marked the beginning of the end of Capone’s reign over Chicago’s underworld. After initially serving time at a federal prison in Atlanta, he was transferred to the notorious Alcatraz Island in 1934.

Capone was released in 1939 after serving approximately eight years, but his health had deteriorated significantly. He spent his final years at his Florida estate, where he died on Jan. 25, 1947, just days after his 48th birthday.

text:
On 28 October 1986 at Madison Square Garden, Sheila E. smuggled concentrated Minneapolis Sound into Lionel Richie’s “Outrageous” tour.

By late 1986 she was far more than “the percussionist.” Prince had written and produced the bulk of her breakthrough material (The Glamorous Life, “The Belle of St. Mark,” “A Love Bizarre,” “Sister Fate”), released her on Paisley Park, and put her on the Purple Rain and final Parade tour dates. Weeks earlier he began dismantling the Revolution; within months she would become his drummer and musical director for Sign o’ the Times and Lovesexy. This MSG night sat in that hinge.

Richie’s set was polished, romantic stadium pop. Sheila’s roughly 45-minute opening offered the counterpoint: tight, high-energy funk and percussion rather than the more theatrical bits she had sometimes used while opening for Prince. She arrived with a locked-in band, striking clothes, and songs the audience already knew.

Core material from the tour included “The Glamorous Life,” the extended groove of “A Love Bizarre,” “Sister Fate,” “Bedtime Story,” “Holly Rock,” “Love on a Blue Train,” and Prince’s “Erotic City.” Reviews of nearby dates noted her launching the latter with a lusty yelp, then taking the kit for a lengthy athletic solo during “A Love Bizarre.” Percussion work frequently stole the night; an Oklahoma review singled out “Sister Fate,” “Bedtime Story,” “A Love Bizarre,” and a “Glamorous Life” encore.

What separated her from other Prince-associated performers was the playing. Daughter of jazz percussionist Pete Escovedo and already a veteran of George Duke, Marvin Gaye, and Richie tours, she treated the drums and timbales with precision and power, not as props. She largely left neon sticks and cartoonish elements behind and concentrated on the music—muscular Minneapolis funk delivered with Oakland chops.

She later reappeared in Richie’s set for a few numbers, reinforcing the pre-solo professional relationship. Contemporary accounts of the MSG run noted a clean, well-rehearsed opening in front of a full house. The night itself was interrupted by the Mets’ World Series game on portable TVs, but Sheila’s set was already finished.
From a Prince-centric view, the show proved the catalog he had written for her translated to large arenas outside his own tours, that the percussionist he trusted could command a stage, and that the future drummer of his most ambitious live bands was already operating at a high level. The sensuality and rhythmic complexity cut through the more wholesome Richie atmosphere without needing the Purple One himself onstage.

Madison Square Garden got a concentrated hit of the Minneapolis Sound from its most skilled living emissary. Sheila E. didn’t merely support Lionel Richie; she showed why Prince had put her out front—and why he would soon put her behind the kit again.

In 1822, William Johnson of Charleston, South Carolina who President Thomas Jefferson nominated to be an associate justice of the United States Supreme Court, authored the two-volume “Sketches of the Life and Correspondence of Nathanael Greene,” a comprehensive work about Major General Nathanael Greene. Greene, a native of Rhode Island, was an early volunteer in the American revolutionary cause who rose rapidly through the ranks, eventually becoming one of George Washington’s most trusted advisors and military commanders. Greene was, by any possible measure, an important figure in the successful conduct of the Revolution. Johnson’s biography—a massive work running to more than one thousand pages—was the first systematic account of Greene’s life and was written with the support of his family and the benefit of access to Greene’s papers.

On October 27, 1822, Thomas Jefferson wrote to William Johnson who had sent him a copy of his narrative of General Greene. Jefferson offered “[his] thanks... until I could have time to read it” and could “express the gratification it has afforded me.” But the reasons for that praise were telling. Jefferson clearly believed that Greene was an important figure and that committing his story to print was a worthwhile objective. Jefferson said that “Greene was truly a great man. He had not perhaps all which so peculiarly rendered General Washington the fittest man on earth for directing so great a contest under so great difficulties.” Jefferson went on to write that Nathanael Greene was “second to no one in enterprise, in resource, in sound judgement, promptitude of decision and every other military talent.”

text:
Yes, there are teacher unions and professional associations in Texas, but they operate under major legal limits that make them much weaker than in most other states.
Main Organizations
•Texas AFT (American Federation of Teachers affiliate): Describes itself as a union with roughly 66,000 members (K-12 educators, higher-ed staff, support personnel, and retirees). It has local affiliates in many districts.
•Texas State Teachers Association (TSTA): The NEA (National Education Association) affiliate. It is commonly described as one of the two main teacher unions in the state.
•Other groups, such as the Association of Texas Professional Educators (ATPE) and Texas Classroom Teachers Association (TCTA), function more as professional associations. They offer similar practical benefits (especially liability insurance and legal help) but are not typically classified the same way as the AFT/NEA-affiliated groups.
Membership is entirely voluntary. Texas is a right-to-work state, so no one can be required to join or pay dues as a condition of employment. Public employees also cannot be denied a job solely because of membership or non-membership in a labor organization.
Key Legal Restrictions
Under Texas Government Code Chapter 617:
•Collective bargaining is prohibited for public employees. State and local officials cannot enter binding contracts with labor organizations over wages, hours, or working conditions. Any such contract is void. School boards set pay scales and policies themselves; a union negotiates no master contract.
•Strikes are illegal for public employees, with severe penalties (including loss of civil-service and reemployment rights). No major organized teacher strikes have occurred in modern Texas history because of these rules.
Some districts allow limited “consultation” with employee groups, but these discussions are non-binding and cannot produce exclusive bargaining rights or contracts. Teachers retain the individual right to present grievances (with or without a representative).
What These Groups Actually Do
Because they cannot bargain for contracts or strike, their main activities are:
•Lobbying the Texas Legislature on funding, pay, benefits, and policy
•Providing professional liability insurance and legal representation for individual members
•Advocating for members in workplace disputes and offering other member services
In rankings of teacher-union strength (e.g., Fordham Institute’s 2026 analysis), Texas ranks near the bottom nationally (around 46th overall, in the weakest tier), especially on bargaining rules and resources/membership.
Bottom line: Teacher unions and associations exist and have tens of thousands of members, but Texas law strips them of the core powers (collective bargaining and the right to strike) that define strong public-sector unions elsewhere. They function primarily as voluntary advocacy and service organizations rather than as traditional bargaining agents.

Label them however you want, but I asked @grok if Texas had teacher unions, and this was the response.

text:
The Australian Nurses Who Never Came Home
by @Catholic_Weekly [HISTORY]

Twenty-one Australian Army nurses who survived a sinking ship only to be murdered on an Indonesian beach will be remembered through prayer and music at Sydney Town Hall on 8 November.

Catholic arts organisation Artes Christi will present Mozart’s Requiem – A Candlelit Tribute to Our Military Nurses, bringing together an 80-strong choir and orchestra ahead of Remembrance Day.

Presented in support of the Australian Remembrance Foundation, the commemoration will honour the nurses killed in the Bangka Island massacre, alongside military nurses across generations, including those serving today.

Organisers are seeking Defence approval for 21 serving military nurses, seven each from Navy, Army and Air Force, to lay 21 wreaths in memory of the women.

A representative of Vivian Bullwinkel’s family is also being invited to participate.

On 16 February 1942, Japanese soldiers ordered 22 Australian Army nurses into the sea at Radji Beach on Bangka Island and opened fire. Twenty-one nurses were killed. Bullwinkel, wounded in the shooting, was the only nurse to survive.

The women had fled Singapore aboard the SS Vyner Brooke as Japanese forces advanced.

When Japanese aircraft sank the ship on 14 February, survivors struggled ashore, with some reaching Radji Beach. After surviving the massacre, Bullwinkel hid before being captured and spent the remainder of the war as a prisoner.

Following her return to Australia, she testified at a war crimes tribunal and devoted herself to nursing and preserving the memory of her murdered colleagues.

Other Australian nurses who survived the sinking endured years of captivity in Japanese camps. Music became one source of consolation for women imprisoned in Sumatra.

Fellow internees Margaret Dryburgh and Norah Chambers established a women’s vocal orchestra, reconstructing classical music from memory and arranging instrumental parts for unaccompanied voices.

Their repertoire included the Largo from Dvořák’s New World Symphony. Amid hunger, illness and confinement, the performances offered prisoners an opportunity to make music together and recall life beyond the camps.

text:
Putin on Su-57: India Was Offered Joint Development

🚨Here’s What Actually Happened

Russian President Vladimir Putin has stated that Russia offered India a joint program to develop the Su-57 fifth-generation fighter. India did not proceed as a full partner, so Russia continued alone. He has also said Moscow remains ready to work with India on the Su-57 (including co-production and further development) without restrictions, and that the same applies to advanced air defence systems such as the S-500.

The original effort was the FGFA (Fifth Generation Fighter Aircraft) program, launched in 2007 under the UPA government of Manmohan Singh. It was based on Russia’s PAK-FA platform, which later became the Su-57. After more than a decade of talks, India formally withdrew in 2018 under the NDA government of Narendra Modi. Senior officials, including NSA Ajit Doval, informed Russia of the decision, and then Defence Minister Nirmala Sitharaman confirmed it. The Indian Air Force had flagged issues around high costs, limited technology transfer, engine readiness, stealth performance, and whether the aircraft met its operational requirements. India had already funded part of the preliminary design phase before exiting.

The exit was therefore not a simple refusal of the original 2007 offer by one government. Problems accumulated over years under both UPA and NDA administrations, and the final decision was taken in 2018. Russia has continued to pitch the Su-57 to India with various co-production and technology-sharing options, while India has focused on its indigenous AMCA program and assessed foreign options carefully.

India-Russia defence ties continue in other areas, including the S-400 systems already delivered. Any future move on the Su-57 or S-500 will depend on cost, technology access, operational fit, and India’s priority of strategic autonomy and domestic manufacturing.

text: The objection to student loan forgiveness is not that anyone suffered, but that cancelling debt does not make it disappear. It transfers it to taxpayers, including people who never went to college, who worked through trade school, who served in the military to earn tuition help, or who sacrificed to pay their own loans in full. That is a strange definition of fairness. It also rewards the most expensive choices: graduate degrees and high-tuition schools gain the most, while future students face even higher prices because colleges learn that Washington will absorb the bill. If the system is broken, fix the system: require price transparency, hold schools accountable for programs that leave graduates unable to repay, expand apprenticeships and trade pathways, and offer income-based repayment that is honest about costs. Blanket forgiveness, by contrast, teaches borrowers and institutions that contracts are optional, punishes responsibility, and leaves the next class to borrow even more. Compassion should mean helping people build earning power and holding colleges to account, not writing off one generation's debt with another generation's taxes. Vote red. God bless!

Another demanded protective gloves, rubber boots, and legal representation.

A third escaped into a nearby technology company, where executives mistook its enthusiastic keyboard pounding for artificial intelligence development and immediately offered it a senior management position.

Municipal officials grew particularly concerned when the remaining primates began removing hazardous debris rather than waiting for the appropriate interagency coordination process.

"These animals appear to believe that when something dangerous is lying on the sidewalk, the correct response is to remove it," an imaginary city spokesperson complained. "That is a dangerously simplistic understanding of contemporary urban policy."

The San Francisco Board of Supervisors consequently commissioned a $125 million study to determine whether the monkeys' preference for unobstructed sidewalks demonstrated unconscious geographical bias.

Researchers were instructed to submit their findings within five years.

By that time, the animals were expected to have retired.

LOS ANGELES: HOLLYWOOD DISCOVERS ITS NEXT FRANCHISE

Los Angeles officials initially welcomed the federal program, provided all participating primates were represented by licensed talent agents and received appropriate screen credits for any footage subsequently distributed through entertainment platforms.

Within 24 hours, Hollywood producers announced competing television projects, including Keeping Up With the Chimpanzees, The Real Primates of Beverly Hills, and America's Next Top Sanitation Monkey.

Netflix allegedly offered $80 million for exclusive streaming rights to a baboon removing an abandoned mattress from a sidewalk. The Screen Actors Guild objected after discovering that the animal had performed dramatic work without union representation.

The controversy intensified when a production company attempted to replace the baboon with a computer-generated version. Animal-rights advocates accused the studio of eliminating legitimate employment opportunities for working primates.

Meanwhile, an imaginary Los Angeles planning commission warned that restoring pedestrian access to neglected sidewalks might accelerate neighborhood gentrification.

The commission recommended preserving 30 percent of the existing garbage as part of the area's established visual character.

Several monkeys ignored the recommendation and were accused of participating in an unauthorized beautification campaign.

Their talent agents immediately terminated negotiations.

MONKEY UNION DEMANDS HAZARD PAY

The administration's most serious labor dispute erupted when representatives of the newly established International Brotherhood of Primates, Local 000, refused to approve further deployments without comprehensive workplace protections.

"These are zoo animals," explained the fictional union president. "They're accustomed to controlled environments, regular veterinary supervision, predictable feeding schedules, and reasonable sanitation standards. You cannot simply send them into downtown San Francisco and expect them to adapt overnight."

The union demanded hazardous-duty compensation, comprehensive medical coverage, psychological counseling, retirement benefits, and guaranteed reassignment to accredited zoological facilities following completion of the program.

Federal negotiators initially offered bananas.

The union demanded organic bananas.

The administration countered with conventional bananas and an unlimited supply of federal commemorative certificates.

Negotiations deteriorated when the union discovered that members of Congress received substantially better benefits despite producing considerably less measurable work.

Trump threatened to replace the entire workforce with squirrels.

"Very hardworking animals. Tremendous energy. And they work for peanuts."

SCIENTISTS DISCOVER AN UNEXPECTED BEHAVIORAL CHANGE

The program's most disturbing development emerged during a federally sponsored behavioral study examining how primates adapted to extended exposure to municipal government.

Researchers discovered that the animals were beginning to imitate the institutional practices surrounding them.

In Seattle, several chimpanzees abandoned their collection equipment and established a nonprofit organization. Rather than removing garbage, they began soliciting donations to increase public awareness about the importance of discussing possible future sanitation initiatives.

Their first fundraising event generated $3.4 million.

In San Francisco, an enterprising primate discovered that municipal research grants offered considerably greater financial rewards than actual sanitation work. It promptly submitted a proposal examining the relationship between discarded packaging and structural inequities in urban waste distribution.

The proposal received unanimous approval.

In Los Angeles, a group of monkeys began filming themselves posing beside garbage bags they had no intention of collecting. Their social media accounts attracted millions of followers, luxury sponsorships, and an invitation to appear at an environmental awards ceremony.

Federal researchers concluded that the animals were demonstrating an alarming capacity for political adaptation.

"We sent these primates into government-controlled environments because we believed they could improve municipal sanitation," explained one imaginary administration scientist. "Instead, we've discovered that government can teach a chimpanzee how to avoid work, acquire funding, and claim credit for results it never produced."

The study recommended immediate intervention before the animals learned to run for public office.

THE PRESIDENT CONSIDERS EXPANDING THE PROGRAM

Despite the complications, Trump reportedly declared Operation Monkey Business an overwhelming success and instructed federal officials to evaluate whether other animals could perform government functions more effectively than their human counterparts.

A proposed second initiative would assign highly trained dolphins to California water management, golden retrievers to congressional ethics investigations, and carrier pigeons to federal agencies struggling with electronic communications.

"Golden retrievers are fantastic," Trump supposedly explained. "Loyal. Honest. They don't take bribes. And when you tell them to fetch something, they actually bring it back. Congress could learn a lot."

Reporters asked whether the administration might eventually replace elected municipal officials with chimpanzees.

The president paused.

"I don't want to insult the monkeys."

THE VERDICT

The fictional premise is absurd, but the underlying question deserves serious consideration: How should citizens evaluate government programs that consume substantial public resources without delivering improvements commensurate with their cost?

Seattle, San Francisco, and Los Angeles face different combinations of homelessness, addiction, sanitation problems, infrastructure deterioration, and public-order challenges. Their causes are complicated, and effective responses require more than collecting garbage. Public spending figures alone cannot establish failure, just as isolated improvements cannot establish comprehensive success. Meaningful accountability requires examining expenditures, measurable outcomes, competing explanations, and whether programs achieve their stated objectives.

Nevertheless, complexity should not provide permanent immunity from scrutiny. Governments routinely measure success through appropriations, staffing levels, program announcements, and administrative activity. Taxpayers are entitled to ask whether those inputs produce identifiable benefits, whether less expensive alternatives were seriously considered, and whether unsuccessful approaches are discontinued or merely reorganized under new names.

The imaginary primates in Operation Monkey Business illustrate the distinction.

When a monkey picks up garbage, the garbage is gone.

When government officials approve another sanitation initiative, the expenditure is immediate, the administrative machinery expands, and the promised improvement may remain years away. Neither the press release nor the appropriation should be confused with the result.

The greatest danger to Operation Monkey Business, however, was never that the monkeys would prove incapable of cleaning America's streets.

It was that they would become so thoroughly accustomed to municipal government that they would eventually stop trying.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

🚨BREAKIMG: ATTENTION PARENTS!

A family doctor in the Chicago area is warning that hospitals are vaccinating children while they are under anesthesia, often without clear, informed consent from parents.

In his own words: “I'm a family doctor who practices in the suburbs and the city of Chicago. I wanted to offer some practical advice tonight to those of you who, like me, might be angry and very concerned about the news reports detailing the rise of what one hospital is calling, close your eyes, we'll immunize. This is a growing practice, perhaps pioneered at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia... where children are undergoing elective and emergency medical surgeries and being immunized while they're away from their parents in the operating room.”

He adds that parents have often given consent unknowingly or under duress, and that true informed consent is rarely being provided the way it should be. Flu shots are the most common, but RSV, COVID, and other vaccines are also being given while kids are sedated.

Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia has run its official “Close Your Eyes, We’ll Immunize” program since 2023 and reported giving 2,054 influenza doses this way in the 2025–2026 season alone. Children’s Hospital Colorado has done it for more than 18,000 patients since 2020. Lurie Children’s in Chicago and other facilities have similar offers, with staff raising the option on the day of surgery.

Imagine taking your child in for appendicitis. You sign a form saying the team can do what’s necessary to help your child. Fifteen minutes later, before the first incision, your child gets a flu shot you never specifically approved. That is the scenario the doctor is describing.

Ask, in writing, before your child goes under. Do not assume a general surgical consent covers vaccines.
